extracted.intended_audience: Australian public, stakeholders and potential participants in Productivity Commission inquiries (governments, industry, community groups, researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the Commission’s role, operating principles, when and how public inquiries and commissioned research are run, and how members of the public and organisations can engage (register, submit, attend hearings). Covers statutory objectives that enquiries should consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use public inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Where policy issues to be addressed by the Commission require extensive public consultation and exposure — either because they may have a significant impact on different groups within society, or are otherwise contentious or complex to assess — they are typically handled through public inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public inquiries are used for matters needing broad consultation, significant-impact or complex/contentious issues. They are widely advertised and rely on active community involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of reference and inquiry duration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Treasurer sends a ‘reference’ to the Commission. The terms of reference outline in writing what the inquiry covers and how long the Commission has to report. In order to allow participants time to prepare submissions and respond to a draft report, including through public hearings, most inquiries specify a duration of 12 months. But more pressing matters can be dealt with in 6 months or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference sets scope and timeline; expect most inquiries to run ~12 months; shorter timelines possible for urgent matters. Timeline choices should accommodate public submission and draft-report response periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide policy options and recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is often required to provide the Government with policy options representing alternative means of addressing the issues, as well as a preferred option. It may also make recommendations on any matters it considers relevant to the inquiry, consistent with its statutory policy guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final reports should present alternative policy options plus a preferred option; recommendations must be consistent with statutory policy instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft report release and further submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission publishes a draft report or position paper and invites further submissions. Hearings are usually held on this preliminary report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders can respond to draft findings; hearings typically take place on the draft to allow further input before finalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation mechanisms and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission’s advice to government, and the information and analysis on which it is based, are all open to public scrutiny. Its processes provide for extensive public input and feedback through hearings, workshops and other consultative forums, and through the release of draft reports and preliminary findings. People can register their interest in an inquiry by various means, including online, and can monitor other participants’ reactions in submissions which are also posted on the Commission’s website. Transcripts of public hearings are available online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register interest online, lodge written submissions (which will be posted), attend hearings/workshops; expect transcripts and published submissions to support transparency and broader scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final report tabled timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Final inquiry reports must be tabled in Parliament within 25 sitting days of the Government receiving the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission must forward final reports to Government in time for tabling within 25 sitting days; stakeholders should be aware of this statutory timing for parliamentary consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government decision-making and uptake of recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is up to governments to make decisions in response to the Commission’s recommendations. Governments are not obliged to follow the Commission’s advice, although in practice more recommendations have been accepted than rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission provides evidence-based recommendations but cannot compel adoption; expect parliamentary and public debate following tabling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages in the inquiry process
rubrics_metrics.description: STAGES IN THE INQUIRY PROCESS: The Australian Government decides to initiate an inquiry; The Treasurer sends a reference to the Commission; The Commission advertises the inquiry and calls for parties to register their interest; The Commission visits interested parties, distributes an issues paper to focus attention on the matters it considers relevant and invites written submissions; Depending on the reference, hearings or other consultative forums will be held; The Commission publishes a draft report or position paper and invites further submissions; Hearings are usually held on this preliminary report; A final report is sent to the Government. Briefings are held and the report is considered by relevant Ministers; The Treasurer tables the report in Parliament. The Government may announce its response at that time or at a later date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential checklist for inquiry lifecycle — useful for planning submissions and participation at each step (issues paper stage, submission, hearings, draft report response, final report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of commissioned research vs formal public inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, the Government may ask the Commission to conduct research on a topic which, while important, is seen as requiring less formal public consultation than a full public inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioned studies typically involve less formal consultation than public inquiries; examples include policy reviews and focused research projects. Stakeholders should monitor calls for input on these projects, but consultation may be more limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission operates under the powers, protection and guidance of its own legislation. Its independence is formally exercised under the Productivity Commission Act through the Chair, Deputy Chair and Commissioners, who are appointed by the Governor-General for fixed periods. The Productivity Commission has its own budgetary allocation and permanent staff, operating at arm’s length from other government agencies. While the Government largely determines its work program, the Commission’s findings and recommendations are based on its own analyses and judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence implies reports and advice are evidence- and analysis-based rather than ministerial direction; stakeholders can expect work produced on the basis of Commission judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as an operating principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission’s advice to government, and the information and analysis on which it is based, are all open to public scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is implemented via publication of draft reports, submissions, hearing transcripts and supporting analysis; this supports accountability and public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-wide perspective requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is obliged under its statutory guidelines to take a broad view, encompassing the interests of the economy and community as a whole, rather than just particular industries or groups. Environmental, regional and social dimensions of its work are also carefully considered, informed by public consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and recommendations should consider economy-wide impacts and distributional, environmental and regional implications, not just narrow sectoral interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: improve the productivity and economic performance of the economy
rubrics_metrics.description: improve the productivity and economic performance of the economy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary statutory objective to inform and recommend policies that raise productivity and economic performance; inquiry work should be assessed against this aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: reduce unnecessary regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: reduce unnecessary regulation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of regulatory proposals should consider whether regulation is necessary and whether removal/reform would improve productivity or reduce burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: encourage efficient and internationally competitive Australian industries
rubrics_metrics.description: encourage the development of efficient and internationally competitive Australian industries
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy options are to be considered for their effect on industry efficiency and international competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: facilitate adjustment to structural change
rubrics_metrics.description: facilitate adjustment to structural change
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations should consider how policies ease transitions for workers, firms and regions affected by structural economic changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: recognise the interests of the community generally and all those likely to be affected
rubrics_metrics.description: recognise the interests of the community generally and all those likely to be affected by its proposals
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses must account for distributional impacts and affected stakeholders; public consultation helps identify those interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: increase employment and promote regional development
rubrics_metrics.description: increase employment and promote regional development
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider employment and regional development effects when evaluating policy options and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: have regard to Australia’s international commitments and trade policies of other countries
rubrics_metrics.description: have regard to Australia’s international commitments and the trade policies of other countries
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy assessments should consider international obligations and foreign trade policy context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative instruction: ensure Australian industry develops in ecologically sustainable ways
rubrics_metrics.description: ensure Australian industry develops in ecologically sustainable ways
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental sustainability must be considered alongside productivity and competitiveness objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual reporting obligations and outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is required under its Act to report annually not only on its activities, but also on industry and productivity performance generally, as well as on the effects of industry assistance and regulation. Its Annual Report Series comprises: The Annual Report (on operations and performance); The Trade & Assistance Review (reports on trade policy and assistance developments and contains the Commission’s latest estimates of government assistance to Australian industries); The Commission also reports on trends in the productivity of the economy — each edition unpacks the latest ABS productivity statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual reporting is a statutory duty covering operations, assistance, trade policy impacts and productivity trends; these reports are sources of Commission analysis and benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance monitoring criteria (Report on Government Services)
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual Report on Government Services (RoGS) provides information on the equity, effectiveness and efficiency of a range of government services, including health, education, justice, housing and community services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance reporting should emphasise balanced, credible comparative information on equity, effectiveness and efficiency to encourage improved service delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Works reviews and evidence-based assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: To compliment the performance reporting in the RoGS, the Secretariat from the Commission undertakes 'What Works' reviews. These review global evidence on what works (or does not) to achieve particular outcomes for government services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and service recommendations should draw on global evidence syntheses about effectiveness; 'What Works' reviews inform practical service-improvement options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-initiated research program guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has a statutory mandate to conduct a program of research to support its inquiries, annual reporting and other responsibilities. The Commission’s program of research is guided by government statements on policy priorities and parliamentary debate and committee work, and by drawing on consultations with various interest groups. The supporting research program emphasises the sustainability of productivity improvements, including environmental and social aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-initiated research topics are selected based on policy priorities, parliamentary debate and stakeholder consultation, with emphasis on sustainable productivity (environmental/social).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive Neutrality Complaints Office (AGCNCO) complaint handling process
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office receives and assesses complaints, proceeds with complaints that warrant investigation and provides independent advice to the Treasurer on each matter. The Government is not obliged to accept this advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AGCNCO assesses admissibility and merit, investigates where warranted, and advises the Treasurer — its advice is independent but not binding on government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may lodge a competitive neutrality complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual, organisation or government body with an interest in the application of competitive neutrality may lodge a complaint, although they are encouraged first to discuss their complaint with AGCNCO staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad standing to lodge complaints; preliminary discussion with staff is recommended to clarify the complaint and process.

rubrics_metrics.name: International linkages and relevance of international evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has international linkages to research and other organisations through appointments of Commissioners and staff, research alliances and participation in various discussion forums. The Commission’s research on productivity and quantification of barriers to trade is drawn on internationally, with its analysis of regulatory policy and applications also attracting particular interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission work is informed by and contributes to international research; comparative and international evidence is relevant to inquiries and research.
